Neutral against Underweight was tested; the data say the consumer slows rather than breaks, so Neutral, with no weight carried in Thematic Fit/Momentum. Component 1 regime, 30-Oct-26 (risk-off beneath a steady index, led now by credit and the cost of debt rather than by the artificial intelligence wash-out alone: the US ten-year above 5% after a hawkish Fed hold with two dissents for a hike, Goldman Sachs' Risk Appetite Indicator at its lowest since April 2025, euro investment-grade and high-yield yields up 30 and 90 basis points since September, Brent near $115, the French premium a record 150 basis points, Europe rotating to quality, defensives and non-AI growth, the STOXX Europe 600 1.7% from its high with breadth recovering from the bottom fifth of three years and defensives leading cyclicals at four weeks and three months; sources present 2026-W44). 22 of the 144 Pool stocks are UK-listed. Counter-case: a 1.0% growth year with a hiking central bank is an Underweight in most books. To D on hawkish guidance on 5-Nov-26, a January price cap above 16% or a spring fiscal event with broad taxes; to B if a second source makes the UK case with the rate path read.

memo.verdict: Neutral; park; conviction medium. BT.A-GB at Triaging, 2026-09-27. The record's thesis: BT is a cash-flow self-help case, not an earnings-growth case; the fibre build has passed its peak, capital expenditure falls by more than £1bn in FY27 and the cost programme takes out £2.2bn more, so normalised free cash flow is targeted to double from £1.5bn in FY26 to about £3.0bn by FY30 while consensus adjusted earnings per share stay at about 18p to 19p. At 196.55p the shares pay 10.25x 24-month-forward earnings (80th percentile of the stock's own five-year range; 88th of ten years on the dashboard) for that cash plan, and the modal return on the framework's convention is about 7% a year at both horizons against the 20% bar. The park is not the gate's (no D or F on management, business quality, predictability or trackability); it is the 'Modal return' at F and the 'Investment Thesis' at D. Progress would follow any one of: the price below about 165p with FY27 guidance intact; the FY28 consensus earnings-per-share line rising 5% or more in a quarter; reported free cash flow after pension deficit payments and restructuring exceeding the dividend by more than £500m at the FY27 result. Invalidation would follow line losses above 950k a year, mandatory margin-squeeze caps in Ofcom's final TAR statement, or pension deficit contributions above £850m a year. The disagreement with the bullish research is about the multiple, not the facts: at 10x the return is about 7% a year; at the conceded 12x it is about 20.0% a year over eighteen months.
case: The record's argument runs from the change to the outputs to the price to the return and the pattern.

The change is internal, broad and real, and the external forces subtract from it. Five of twelve internal forces are strong (chief executive, other leaders, strategy, perimeter reduction, standards improvement), passing the screen's rule of three; the two largest forces, the capital-expenditure step-down (£5,127m in FY26 to £4.2bn to £4.3bn in FY27 and toward about £3.5bn by FY30) and the cost transformation (£1.5bn realised, £3.7bn by FY30, restructuring cash from about £400m to about £100m a year), sit outside the screen's twelve. The false-positive checks mostly pass: not a caretaker, not a slide-deck transformation, cost target raised not trivially, no crown jewel sold, leverage falling, no debt-funded buyback. Not A because no financial guidance has been raised (FY27 targets reconfirmed, revenue target cut in November 2024; FY26 EBITDA scorecard paid 77%) and the change lands in cash. Perimeter reduction is A: five international units sold (£222m net consideration) and the international enterprise business into a 50:50 Verizon joint venture (agreed 29 June 2026; $625m equalisation payment; completion H2 2027), removing about 10% of revenue and 1% to 2% of EBITDA; the cost is extreme domestic concentration. Balance sheet D (deleveraging, not utilisation; 0.5x reduction to BBB+ before enhanced distributions); shareholder returns C (progressive dividend, 8.32p up 2%; buybacks deferred, not before FY28 at the earliest); price rises C (nominal and regulated: fixed £3 and £1.50 rises, or £4.00 and £2.50 in another source; Openreach indexed at 3.6% CPI; Consumer broadband ARPU -2%).

External forces D: four headwinds of seven. Competition D: nexfibre's £2bn Netomnia acquisition (3.2m premises added to 3.4m; CMA Phase 2 by December 2026) and Virgin Media O2's wholesale unit; Sky selling 2.5Gbps and 5Gbps over CityFibre at £35 and £45; VodafoneThree complete with an £11bn plan and MVNO remedies; Openreach lost 825k lines in FY26, guides about 800k, Q1 192k; alt-nets past 20m premises, 47% of premises multi-operator, take-up 16.4%, over £9bn of debt, CityFibre cutting 18% of staff and raising £900m; construction down at least 40%, a shift 'from construction to consolidation'. Political and regulatory D: TAR26 settled to 2031 with the 'fair bet' reaffirmed and no cost-based controls in 86% of premises, but Ofcom's 28 July 2026 provisional block of the £9.50 'Incremental New to Openreach' offer is the first halt of an Openreach pricing scheme; anchor product ceiling cut from £22.37 to £17.17 with a £100m FY27 working-capital drag; the £50 geographic bounty and £19.32-capped Frontbook offer cleared; final decision September or October 2026, 'mandatory margin squeeze caps' the earnings review's thesis-breaker. Demand D: UK broadband flat at 28.6m lines for four years; legacy voice loss £150m to £200m a year; PSTN switch-off January 2027. Macro D: ten-year gilt yields near 5% on £19,966m of net debt and the pension; June 2026 triennial sets contributions from autumn 2026. Catch-all C: TalkTalk about 2.7m to 2.8m lines, 95% on Openreach, about £1bn a year, in a sale process; Deutsche Bank calls a migration 'a material unpriced risk event'. Supply side B (about £300 per premise; energy 88% hedged FY27; engineering headcount 38,000 toward 30,000; payroll taxes about £100m a year against). Disruption C (Starlink partnership; Ofcom accepts Starlink's £40 service for universal service; fixed wireless to 3.7m more premises; AI on cost).
counter_case: The strongest case against, the risks report's 'false friend', is that the cash inflection is optical. As capital expenditure falls, the £600m-plus of own-work capitalised labour returns to operating expense (Redburn sizes a £1bn capital-expenditure cut at about £600m of decapitalisation), compressing EBITDA while the cash line looks better; 30% of FY26 normalised free cash flow came from working-capital programmes that reverse, and factoring and supply-chain finance rose from £68m to £476m in a year; cash tax steps up from FY28 as full-expensing losses are used; the £780m a year of pension deficit payments never enter the measure the company reports and management is paid on (adjusted EBITDA 27.5% and normalised free cash flow 27.5% of incentives, the two measures that exclude the pension top-ups and specific items, so the measure the market rewards and the measure management is paid on are the same measure and neither is the shareholder's cash). Meanwhile a scaled second wholesaler forms (nexfibre-Netomnia plus Virgin Media O2's upgrade), TalkTalk's roughly £1bn a year of Openreach payments are in play, Sky is already multi-sourcing, and since 28 July 2026 the regulator has removed Openreach's nationwide discount. On the bears' arithmetic Openreach share drifts toward 50% over a decade, EBITDA margins compress 150 basis points, reported free cash flow falls 15%, leverage rises to 3.5x, and the equity is worth 100p at 5x FY27 earnings (Deutsche Bank 150p; Morgan Stanley's bear 100p; options in mid-2026 gave a 4.4% probability of below 100p). The evidence is real: specific items £867m; net debt up £150m with the dividend paid; the Telia and Orange precedents (Orange's 2012 cut, -14%, -20 percentage points against peers; Telia's vendor-financing cover problem); BT's own 2016 to 2024 history, in which the Italian accounting scandal began an eight-year decline, Business revenue fell 21% and EBITDA 45% between 2020 and 2024, the dividend was suspended in May 2020 and rebased to 7.7p from 15.4p, and the shares doubled in six months after the suspension then halved over two years after reinstatement. A 41.7% EBITDA margin that rose every year while revenue fell is partly a capitalisation effect. The multiple doubled from 5.66x to 10.25x on falling earnings, a plausible fit with 'paying up for a turn that is in cash, not earnings'. The dividend was not covered by the shareholder's cash in FY26.

The record concedes the mechanism in full: normalised free cash flow is not shareholder cash, and the record uses the shareholder's cash wherever cover is tested; the own-work-capitalised reversal is real and is the one thing that could turn the margin line down while cash rises; the cash-tax step-up is real from FY28; the wholesale base is eroding at about 4% a year and the regulator has just made it harder to defend; the accounting point about the margin is conceded too.
triggers: - Progress triggers (any one): price below about 165p with FY27 guidance intact (the modal path clears 20% a year at eighteen months; 153p at the blend; 140p at three years); the FY28 consensus earnings-per-share line (0.197 GBP mean at 2026-09-25) rising 5% or more in a quarter; reported free cash flow after pension deficit payments and restructuring exceeding the dividend by more than £500m at the FY27 result.

- Invalidate levels: Openreach line losses above 950k in a year (the earnings review's trigger); mandatory margin-squeeze caps in Ofcom's final TAR statement; pension deficit contributions above £850m a year (the review's secondary trigger); normalised free cash flow below £1.7bn at the FY27 result; a year-on-year decline in Openreach broadband ARPU.

- Alarm levels: line losses above 220k in any quarter; normalised free cash flow below £1.9bn at the FY27 result, or £2.0bn achieved with more than £300m of working-capital and factoring inflows; Openreach broadband ARPU growth below 4%; any language in Ofcom's final statement about ex-ante margin controls; any announced migration by Sky or by TalkTalk's acquirer; the 24-month-forward multiple below 9.0x with earnings unchanged; a 5% cut to FY28 consensus earnings per share over three months.

- The five things the case turns on, with the record's odds: FY27 normalised free cash flow of about £2.0bn arriving, probable, about three chances in four; Openreach line losses at or below about 850k a year and not accelerating in FY28, plausible to probable, about two in three; Ofcom's final decision confined to blocking the £9.50 offer with no margin-squeeze constraint, likely, about seven in ten; earnings per share growing 3% or more a year from FY28 as depreciation follows capital expenditure down, plausible, about even; the multiple holding at about 10x rather than reverting toward 8.3x, a little better than even, about 55%, because the first three run through Openreach and are not independent.

- Dated events: Ofcom's final decision, September or October 2026; H1 FY27 results, 29 October 2026 (line losses, Business EBITDA, working-capital content of cash); pension triennial outcome from autumn 2026; 25m FTTP premises by December 2026; CMA Phase 2 decision on nexfibre-Netomnia by December 2026; PSTN switch-off 31 January 2027; FY27 results May 2027 (the £2.0bn print); Verizon joint venture completion and $625m payment H2 2027; copper price freedom from April 2029 in 90%-fibre areas; BBB+ metrics and the first buyback, FY29 at the earliest on consensus debt.

- Open questions the record could not close from what was read: overlap with the firm's own historical errors (no track-record or lessons file; the likely overlapping pattern is 'incumbent telecom on a cash-yield thesis'); Wisdom Library archetypes (not in the folder; the research names 'false friend', dividend-cover failure and post-scandal value destruction); live thematics (no file); the pension scheme's response to gilt yields (a decision, not quantifiable); the Openreach revenue basis gap in FactSet (external revenue only, company £6.2bn used); the FactSet free-cash-flow line (137 GBPm against 944 GBPm on the block's own definition; the company's normalised figure used).
